Please use this package to correct Wishweave Wonders Level 1 in the EXISTING project. Preserve a recoverable branch/checkpoint. Keep the approved Purl/Loop identities, rich crochet loom-city setting and existing useful game rules. The required change is a connected running race with natural controllable movement.

THE EXACT PROBLEM
In the supplied recording 6746.mp4, around 0:36–0:37 a blurred pillar wipes from one picture-like section to the next while Purl moves across it without a floor. Similar transitions recur later. I want Purl and Loop to RUN through a real connected path into the next part of the same level, continuously, until the exit. Merely hiding the cut, moving the old picture faster, or attaching another picture behind it does not satisfy this.

FIRST INSPECT, THEN REUSE
Inspect the current world representation, route system, camera, renderer, character animation, touch input and Android host. Identify what can be retained and whether the current renderer can actually support connected geometry. Do not claim the root cause from screenshots alone. If a renderer change is necessary, explain its specific scope and reuse plan before expanding it. The source snippets in this kit are references, not drop-in replacements for an uninspected engine.

USE THE PACKAGE CORRECTLY
1. The three new images in references/ are visual targets. Legacy background images are material/landmark references, not the world renderer.
2. scenery/level1-connected-layout.glb is a genuine simplified 3D layout: connected road top, branch/rejoin and landmarks. It is a BLOCKOUT, not final art. Use it as a spatial foundation or adapt the route contract to the current engine. Add production materials, decorations, colliders and tested feature placement. Maintain continuous top surfaces and safe turn radii.
3. art/ contains existing 2D alpha images of Purl, Loop, Snagling, items and UI, preserved from the earlier visual kit. Review their edges, posing, scale and pivots. Do not mistake them for rigged 3D characters. Prefer a proper rig for this turning camera; if using directional sprites, provide adequate directional views and stable foot anchors and prove the result in motion. Never simulate the complete run by rocking one rear-facing image.
4. code/ contains touch intents and movement/route reference math with tests. Integrate against the real game's state, collisions and animation system. The tests do not establish that the Android build is correct.

CONTROLS AND MOVEMENT
Both characters normally auto-run at a moderately brisk pace. The user controls Purl; Loop is an independent computer rival, identified as such. Swipe left/right changes lateral position smoothly inside the walkable width; near a junction it selects the announced branch. A swipe must never teleport Purl onto an unrelated route or off an edge. At a bend the path heading turns the character naturally. Swipe up triggers one jump with a visible launch, arc, contact shadow and landing. Double-tap toggles a brief controlled deceleration to stop, then resumes on the next double-tap. Loop keeps racing during this player brake. Global Pause freezes the entire simulation. If Purl is stationary, swipe up may jump in place; it must not also resume forward movement. Provide accessible Left/Right/Jump/Run-Stop buttons in addition to gestures.

Run animation must follow actual distance and velocity: alternating contact, push-off, swing and landing; arms opposing legs; mild body rise/fall and lean; heading following the route; stable root and foot contact on the ground. Stopping blends into a real idle pose, with no jogging/hopping in place. Running speed, gait rate and camera speed must be calibrated together on the real device. A natural run may have an airborne phase; do not force both feet onto the floor in every frame. Do not merely double sprite translation speed.

ONE CONTINUOUS LEVEL
Follow the same road from the opening ramp around the tower, through a visible branch/rejoin and tassel section, past the Snagling landing, butterfly area and flower gate. The next area appears ahead before it is entered. Camera follows smoothly behind/above Purl, keeping him readable at roughly 15–20% screen height; it does not repeatedly let him shrink far away then reset to the foreground. Nearby scenery has correct perspective and depth; pillars occlude racers when appropriate. Keep ground contact on the actual road top, not its sidewalls, gold rim or sky. Preserve three distinct collectible types/locations, physical pickups and immediate objective/counter updates.

RIVAL AND EXISTING FEATURES
Loop has his own progress, route decisions and reaction timing. Braking Purl must allow Loop to pass; a valid shorter route or Loop's visible mistake may let Purl regain ground. Do not mirror player speed, teleport the opponent or force a 0.1-second player victory. Show enough shared road and rejoin opportunities to read the race. Keep the existing Snagling wrap/drop/recovery and butterfly animation where they work, integrate them into the continuous course, and reduce unnecessary forced stops. One forgiving opening pull lesson is acceptable; do not turn every later feature into a long static gate. Give a surprise enemy a reachable evasive response, rather than unavoidable damage.

ANDROID AND FINISH
Render across the intended Android app surface with responsive camera/HUD layout and safe cutout/system-gesture insets. No side gutters or clipping characters into them. Do not stretch the artwork. Keep saved rewards small and clear of feet/actions. Real cash out is not implemented by these visual assets; retain the locked placeholder unless separately specified and built. Put the finish trigger on a clearly visible line at the flower-gate threshold. Require the three distinct threads and actual crossing before declaring that racer finished. Record each racer independently.

WORK AND PROOF ORDER
First deliver a working connected opening through the next area, with the target materials/character quality represented honestly. Provide a playable build plus an uninterrupted recording from that exact branch/commit. Demonstrate left/right, jump, braking with Loop passing, resume, the opening bend and entry into the next area without a wipe. Show ground-contact/debug geometry separately if diagnosing placement. Record the normal view as well. Name the actual device/emulator and viewport; do not claim testing on all Android phones.

Stop at that reviewable milestone before broadening a renderer rewrite. Report remaining work and any asset gap explicitly. Once the foundation is accepted, carry it through the complete Level 1 and run docs/ACCEPTANCE.txt, including the three pickups, hit/recovery and finish. A static render, image slideshow, authoring overlay or passing isolated unit test is not a completed playable level. Do not generate another large decorative asset kit to avoid fixing the world and movement.

definition.name: Workflow
definition.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

You've sent a new package that changes direction: replacing the picture-to-picture world with one connected running course. Your prompt asks me to inspect first, explain the reuse plan, then build only the connected opening through the next area and stop there for your review.

I'll start by saving a recoverable checkpoint of the current game. Then I'll unpack the package into its own folder and look at exactly what it contains.

lines: +A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

+When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.
+Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
+- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
+- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
+- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
+- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify
+For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

+**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

+Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.
+Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
+    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
+    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
+      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
+      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
+  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})

+The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

+- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).

+- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.

+- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
+- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
+- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display

+- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.

+- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.

+- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

+Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
+Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

+Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

+Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

+Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.
+DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.
+A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
+- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
+- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
+- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison
+- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
+- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
+- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.
+  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
+that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

+Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.
+When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
+  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
+  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
+  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))
+    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
+Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
+    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
+Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
+    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
+    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
+    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
+        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
+  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.
+Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
+- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
+      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))

+- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.

+- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
+- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.

+- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
+- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
+- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

+Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.
+These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).
+Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

+The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

content.content:
=================== START-HERE.txt
WISHWEAVE WONDERS — CONNECTED WORLD HANDOFF

Send CLAUDIA-PROMPT.txt and all numbered ZIP packages together. Extract all parts into the same folder; they share the Wishweave-Connected-World-Kit directory. Open index.html to review the images, course plan and asset catalog. The HTML is a handoff viewer, not the finished game. Its images live alongside it, so do not send the HTML alone.

The target is a continuous, moderately brisk race from the opened rug to the flower gate. The camera follows Purl around real connected bends into each area. Replace the transition seen around 0:36–0:37 in recording 6746.mp4; do not preserve the old scene-by-scene motion.

READY IN THIS PACKAGE
- Three current mobile-screen concept targets: opening, connected turn, finish.
- Existing Purl, Loop, Snagling, prop, feature and UI images, with alpha and source provenance. Individual art conversions preserve the decoded RGBA pixels.
- A real GLB connected-course BLOCKOUT, route data, generator and overhead map. It establishes broad supported roads, a branch/rejoin and landmark positions from beginning to end.
- An engine-independent touch input module and automated gesture tests.
- A route sampler and distance-driven motion reference, plus tests.
- Clear controls, animation/camera requirements and acceptance checks.

STILL PRODUCTION WORK
The GLB is simplified layout geometry, not the detailed finished city shown in the concept images. It has no rigged characters, final knit textures, full game rules, installed Android app, payout system or certified device performance. The existing character images are 2D poses, not a complete rotation-ready 3D animation rig. Their original edges/pivots require review. This package is useful source material and a construction foundation; it is not proof that Claudia's existing game has been fixed.

CURRENT CONTROLS
Automatic running. Swipe left/right to steer within the path or select a branch. Swipe up to jump. Double-tap to stop/resume Purl only; Loop continues. The separate Pause button pauses both racers and the world. Button equivalents must remain available. Swipe up does not also mean 'start moving'; that would conflict with jump.

FIRST PROOF
Before extending the renderer through the whole level, demonstrate the opened rug, tower bend, branch/rejoin and entry into the next area in one uncut playable run. Keep both runners grounded and readable, with real overtaking and no wipes. Then complete the remaining connected course. Preserve existing work in source control. Read docs/ACCEPTANCE.txt.

IMAGE PRIORITY
references/01-opening-target.webp, 02-connected-turn-target.webp and 03-finish-target.webp are the current visual direction. references/legacy-world-art contains older background paintings for materials and landmark design ONLY. Never turn those paintings back into disconnected gameplay pages. The final geometry must be adapted to be physically traversable; a single painted view cannot define every unseen side of a 3D world.
=================== docs/ACCEPTANCE.txt
ACCEPTANCE — VERIFY THE RUNNING BUILD, NOT JUST THE CONCEPT IMAGES

FIRST CONNECTED STRETCH
1. Start on the opened rug. Run around the tower and onto the next connected area without any cut, page wipe, teleport or sudden perspective/character-size reset.
2. Debug recording: show actual walkable mesh/top boundaries, root contact point and intended route under the same camera. Grounded root stays on the surface; planted feet/shadow agree. Then record the same path in normal view.
3. Test left/right steering at a straight, bend and junction. Show lane movement/branch choice visibly, with no unsupported crossing or edge clipping.
4. Swipe up once: one jump. Land onto the path. Swipe up while stopped: optional jump in place, no unexpected auto-resume.
5. Double-tap: Purl brakes to idle. Loop keeps progressing and can pass. Double-tap again: Purl accelerates and resumes. Pause button freezes both; resume preserves positions.
6. Gestures on UI do not steer/brake the player. A swipe is not interpreted as one of the taps in a double-tap. Pointer cancellation and a second finger do not create phantom gestures.
7. Running looks grounded and directional at ordinary, accelerated and braking speeds. No whole-body waddle used as the only motion; no in-place run when stopped. Both runners satisfy the same motion quality.

WHOLE LEVEL
8. Collect three distinct required threads in separated locations. Counters and instructions update on collection. A repeated pickup cannot substitute for a missing type. Each item is physically reachable from the course.
9. Demonstrate both avoiding Snagling and being hit. On hit, wrapping, inventory change, dropped item and recovery agree. Recovering restores the correct type; no double award. Test the agreed zero-inventory outcome explicitly.
10. Butterfly release remains connected to the course. Avoid long repeated full-stop gates that remove the race pacing. Keep route/obstacle visibility during effects.
11. Main and branch rejoin safely. No decorative posts/landmarks block the walkable route by accident. Show correct pillar/runner depth ordering.
12. Reach the visible flower-gate finish line with three distinct items and cross it before completion. Stop/celebrate appropriately. Award Loop's finish independently; explain if a loss is possible. Test a run in which Loop wins.
13. Saved rewards/cash-out status is honest. Do not infer real payouts from the placeholder bar. If rewards are added later, verify a separate settlement flow.

DISPLAY AND EVIDENCE
14. Test at least the original recording ratio (720 x 1602), a narrower portrait viewport and the user's actual Android device or a named emulator. Verify cutout/system-gesture safe areas, visible collectibles, reachable 48dp-equivalent controls, and all result controls. UI stays clear of feet and the immediate course. This is not universal Android certification.
15. Keep the same uncut gameplay recording and runnable build tied to a named branch/commit. Show inputs. Give actual frame-time observations on tested hardware; do not claim performance from screenshots.

CURRENT KIT VERIFICATION
Local unit tests cover only pure input/route/motion behavior. Layout validation covers the generated blockout mesh and route, not the existing game, character grounding, final artwork, collisions or Android deployment. Track all remaining integration work explicitly.
=================== docs/MOTION-AND-CAMERA.txt
NATURAL MOVEMENT TARGET — DESIGN CONTRACT, NOT A COMPLETED ANIMATION

Purl is the coral player with one curled tuft. Loop is the teal rival with two loops. Preserve their soft round yarn proportions. Their speed should feel like a normal casual running race: lively, with time to react. Calibrate world meters/second, camera distance and stride length together; a hardcoded speed without a known character scale is not a quality guarantee.

Locomotion states: idle, accelerate/run, controlled brake, jump, land, stumble/snared, recover, pull-interaction, finish. Idle has subtle breathing, not repeated two-foot hops. A grounded run has alternating stance and swing with push-off, opposite arm movement, gentle forward lean and limited body bob. Feet may leave the ground during a real run's flight phase. Align every stance foot with the actual projected ground plane. Drive gait phase by distance traveled, not wall-clock time while stationary. Stop the gait when movement stops. A jump uses a separate arc/animation and suppresses run-foot planting until landing.

The current 2D run-left/run-right filenames describe alternate foot poses; do not assume they are left/right-facing turn views. One mirrored rear sprite cannot provide every turn viewpoint. Either build a complete directional set with consistent scale and foot anchors or use a rigged 3D model with grounded animation. The included images are identity/material/pose references, not a finished skeletal run cycle. Review existing alpha edges before final use.

Grounding: position = sampled road center + right-vector * lateral offset + road-up * jump height. The character root/foot anchor is defined in world space. Width bounds include body clearance and railing clearance. Inspect actual visible surface boundaries in debug, not only a route line. Account for the inclined road normal when placing soles/shadows. Respect depth ordering; a foreground pillar must hide the player when it lies between camera and player. No feet on a vertical carpet side, unsupported gap or transition divider.

Steering: a swipe selects a smooth lateral target rather than teleporting. At a junction, lock the pending branch only in a clear decision window; blend position/heading onto the chosen physical route. Keep main and branch progress in comparable race-distance coordinates. Apply the same physical road/collision rules to Loop. Camera follows actual world position, not scene-page progress.

Chase camera: slightly above and behind, aim a short distance ahead along the route. Smooth position and heading with time-based damping, retain enough look-ahead for a bend, avoid clipping through towers. Keep Purl readable near lower-middle and the next action visible. Maintain world continuity when track material changes. No fade, wipe, page slide or scene reset between areas. Do not hold both racers visible by teleporting Loop; use suitable shared/rejoining route design and a small honest lead indicator if needed.

Input: default auto-run; left/right swipe steers or queues a branch; up swipe jumps; double-tap toggles player running/braking. A double-tap is not Pause. UI buttons do not count as gameplay gestures. Multi-touch/cancel must not produce stale actions. Provide button alternatives. Android back/background lifecycle pause is handled by the app host; do not resume the simulation behind a modal or system screen.

The route sampler and input module are reusable implementation examples. They do not provide physics, foot IK, root-motion animation, full opponent AI, Android lifecycle integration or production performance by themselves.
=================== docs/ASSET-GAPS.txt
WHAT THESE ASSETS CAN AND CANNOT DO

The three current mobile-screen images establish the art direction, framing and intended feeling. They are concept renders, not captures of a running application. They cannot prove animation, touch response, continuity or Android fit.

The GLB is an actual connected 3D construction layout with named geometry. It can establish a supported route and landmarks in an engine. Its flat materials and simple landmark shapes are deliberate blockout representations. Finishing it requires the crochet surface materials, embroidered decoration, towers, rails, architecture, clouds, lighting and scenery dressing shown in the references. Distant paintings may be used as background art, but never as sequential pages that the racers traverse without a 3D floor.

The 47 reusable art images are 2D with transparency where supplied. They preserve the source art's decoded pixels. They do not provide skeletons, skin weights, foot IK, motion capture, complete turn-around views or production animation clips. Purl and Loop have several rear-view poses and a front reference. Existing run-left and run-right filenames identify different foot phases, not camera directions. Do not turn a rear pose sideways to fake a curved route.

For a moving camera and natural running, the preferred production solution is properly modeled and rigged Purl and Loop that match the supplied shapes, colors and yarn treatment. A directional-sprite alternative is acceptable only if adequate views, pivots, depth and ground contact are demonstrated in motion. Character identities are fixed: Purl is red with one loop tuft; Loop is teal with two loop-like ear tufts; Snagling is the purple tangled yarn creature.

No final rug deformation system is supplied. A rug must unroll on the supported road, with its top height and collision synchronized; Purl's feet must stay on that top surface. Completing an animation while letting the character float along the previous painted route is not acceptable.

Do not claim these files make a pixel-identical mobile game automatically. Match the visual targets closely while making the geometry physically coherent; disclose any required asset creation or visible design compromise. Review an actual moving opening segment before applying the solution across the whole level.

=================== scenery/README.md
# Wishweave Level 1 — connected spatial blockout

**BLOCKOUT ONLY.** `level1-connected-layout.glb` is real glTF 2.0 3D geometry: one continuous gently sloping main ribbon, one connected branch/rejoin, and named simple landmark geometry. It still needs approved textured ornamental production art matching the separate loomcity target. It is not a finished game or production scenery asset. There are no image plates, textures, rigged characters, colliders, AI, or controls.

## Files

- `level1-connected-layout.glb` — engine-neutral binary glTF spatial scaffold.
- `route.json` — authoritative centerlines, arc lengths, widths, sections, spawns, collectible positions, branch links, and finish coordinates.
- `course-overhead.svg` — exact X/Z overhead projection of the same route data.
- `validation.json` — generated topology, slope, continuity, mesh, and placement checks.
- `generate_course.py` — deterministic reusable generator; Python 3 and NumPy only.

Run `python generate_course.py --output .` from this directory to regenerate all outputs. The script defaults to its own directory. It overwrites only the listed generated outputs.

## Spatial contract

World units are meters, Y is up, and +Z is forward. Main route is 201.319 m long and 6 m wide; branch is 19.543 m long and 2.6 m wide. All `s` values are dense-reference 3D arc length in meters; summing the exported sample chords differs by less than 4 mm over each complete route. Main samples are at most 0.5 m apart; branch samples at most 0.25 m apart. `points` contain `x`, `y`, `z`, `s`, `width`, `tangent`, and `sectionId`. `y` is deck surface elevation. Interpolate between samples, then apply the controller's own grounded/foot offset. Tangent is unit 3D forward; horizontal right is `normalize([tangent.z, 0, -tangent.x])`.

`mainRoute.spawn` and `spawnPositions.player` are the same ground reference. `mainRoute.finish`, top-level `finish`, the Flowergate node origin, and `Finish_Trigger_Origin` use the same endpoint. The visible finish band extends 1.2 m backward from that endpoint with a tiny render offset. A controller should detect crossing the finish plane or `s >= mainRoute.length`, not proximity to a decorative support.

`branches[0].startS` and `endS` address the main route. Its `points[].s` is local branch distance; `points[].mainS` gives monotonically increasing equivalent main-route progress. The `from` and `to` positions exactly match main samples. `connectivity` explicitly links both junctions. The bypass intentionally overlaps the main deck at fork/rejoin to guarantee connected surface; collision union/baking and engine playtesting remain required. This is not a ready-made production collision mesh.

Six sections divide the same unbroken road; they are metadata ranges, not separate rooms. Landmark solids sit off the 6 m floor; arch/gate crossbars are overhead. The Snagling landing and butterfly banner are location placeholders, not characters or behavior. Collectible markers occur at 15% red, 52% teal, and 80% gold.

## Verification and handoff

Generated checks currently pass: max main slope 2.541°, max branch slope 0.197°, minimum main horizontal bend radius 23.124 m. The main ribbon outline has no self intersections. Mesh indices, nondegenerate faces, finite positions, and unit vertex normals are checked. # Wishweave Level 1 — connected spatial blockout

**BLOCKOUT ONLY.** `level1-connected-layout.glb` is real glTF 2.0 3D geometry: one continuous gently sloping main ribbon, one connected branch/rejoin, and named simple landmark geometry. It still needs approved textured ornamental production art matching the separate loomcity target. It is not a finished game or production scenery asset. There are no image plates, textures, rigged characters, colliders, AI, or controls.

## Files

- `level1-connected-layout.glb` — engine-neutral binary glTF spatial scaffold.
- `route.json` — authoritative centerlines, arc lengths, widths, sections, spawns, collectible positions, branch links, and finish coordinates.
- `course-overhead.svg` — exact X/Z overhead projection of the same route data.
- `validation.json` — generated topology, slope, continuity, mesh, and placement checks.
- `generate_course.py` — deterministic reusable generator; Python 3 and NumPy only.

Run `python generate_course.py --output .` from this directory to regenerate all outputs. The script defaults to its own directory. It overwrites only the listed generated outputs.

## Spatial contract

World units are meters, Y is up, and +Z is forward. Main route is 201.319 m long and 6 m wide; branch is 19.543 m long and 2.6 m wide. All `s` values are dense-reference 3D arc length in meters; summing the exported sample chords differs by less than 4 mm over each complete route. Main samples are at most 0.5 m apart; branch samples at most 0.25 m apart. `points` contain `x`, `y`, `z`, `s`, `width`, `tangent`, and `sectionId`. `y` is deck surface elevation. Interpolate between samples, then apply the controller's own grounded/foot offset. Tangent is unit 3D forward; horizontal right is `normalize([tangent.z, 0, -tangent.x])`.

`mainRoute.spawn` and `spawnPositions.player` are the same ground reference. `mainRoute.finish`, top-level `finish`, the Flowergate node origin, and `Finish_Trigger_Origin` use the same endpoint. The visible finish band extends 1.2 m backward from that endpoint with a tiny render offset. A controller should detect crossing the finish plane or `s >= mainRoute.length`, not proximity to a decorative support.

`branches[0].startS` and `endS` address the main route. Its `points[].s` is local branch distance; `points[].mainS` gives monotonically increasing equivalent main-route progress. The `from` and `to` positions exactly match main samples. `connectivity` explicitly links both junctions. The bypass intentionally overlaps the main deck at fork/rejoin to guarantee connected surface; collision union/baking and engine playtesting remain required. This is not a ready-made production collision mesh.

Six sections divide the same unbroken road; they are metadata ranges, not separate rooms. Landmark solids sit off the 6 m floor; arch/gate crossbars are overhead. The Snagling landing and butterfly banner are location placeholders, not characters or behavior. Collectible markers occur at 15% red, 52% teal, and 80% gold.

Mesh indices, nondegenerate faces, finite positions, and unit vertex normals are checked. These are geometric checks; visual fidelity, camera clearance, animation, physics, gameplay and accessibility still require implementation and engine review.

# Touch input handoff `touch-input.mjs` is a small, dependency-free browser ES module. It emits immutable intentions; the game engine owns movement, animation, collision, and race state. Serve these files with the rest of the game; no CDN or runtime network request is needed. Browser ES modules generally need an HTTP origin, so opening the HTML directly as `file://` is not a supported launch method. ## Exports | Export | Contract | | --- | --- | | `attachTouchInput(surface, onIntent, options?)` | Pointer Events adapter. Returns `{ reset, dispose }`; call `dispose()` when replacing the scene. | | `createGestureMachine(options?)` | DOM-free state machine with `down`, `move`, `up`, `cancel(pointerId, options?)`, `reset`. Each returns an array of zero or one intents. | | `classifyGesture(sample, options?)` | Pure classifier: `tap`, `left`, `right`, `jump`, `reserved`, or `none`. | | `swipeThreshold(viewportWidth, options?)` | Horizontal/vertical threshold in CSS pixels. | | `INTENTS` | `left`, `right`, `jump`, `togglePlayerBrake`, `toggleGlobalPause`. Buttons and other accessible controls use the same objects. | | `DEFAULTS` | Frozen gesture defaults; pass overrides only after device testing. | Pointer samples use `{ pointerId, x, y, time, viewportWidth }`. `down` also accepts `ignored: true`. Use CSS coordinates and a single monotonic millisecond clock (`performance.now()`). The adapter supplies these; it deliberately does not depend on browser event timestamp origins. The pure classifier takes `{ dx, dy, duration, maxDistance, viewportWidth }`, where `maxDistance` is the furthest excursion from the starting point. For capture loss while a pointer remains down, call `cancel(id, { retainPointer: true })`; ordinary `pointercancel` uses `cancel(id)`. ## Exact behavior The swipe threshold is 8% of viewport width, clamped to 24–72 CSS pixels. A swipe must have a dominant axis (1.2× the other axis). Each stroke resolves once on release. Left/right emit one steering intention; up emits **jump only**. Down is reserved and emits nothing. Ambiguous diagonals and subthreshold movements emit nothing. Double tap requires two taps of at most 200 ms, each staying within 10 CSS pixels of its start, with releases no more than 320 ms apart and starts within 24 CSS pixels. A single tap has no action. Swipes, long presses, drag-return gestures, UI input, cancellation, and multi-touch invalidate pending taps. After a double tap, a third tap starts a new pair. Two simultaneous contacts are never a double tap. Multi-touch cancels until every tracked contact lifts; the module does not interpret pinch gestures. UI elements marked `data-ui`, native buttons/links/form inputs, editable text, and `role="button"` are excluded. Interaction outside the surface also clears pending taps. Pointer capture, `pointercancel`, capture loss, page visibility, and focus loss are handled. Call `reset()` when switching modes or opening/closing a pause screen. ## Wire the engine Start Purl automatically at a **normal, brisk** running pace. Calibrate world speed to scenery, camera scale, obstacle spacing, and available reaction distance; this module intentionally specifies no numeric world speed. | Intent | Required engine response | | --- | --- | | `{ type: 'steer', direction: -1 or 1 }` | During a junction selection window, queue the corresponding branch and commit at the junction. Between junctions, update the lane target or smooth steering target. Do not treat a swipe as teleportation. | | `{ type: 'jump' }` | Request a jump subject to grounded/jump rules. Never also issue forward movement or a speed boost. | | `{ type: 'toggle-player-brake' }` | Toggle Purl's requested running/stopped state. Decelerate to rest over **0.18–0.25 seconds**; a second double tap resumes normal running. **Loop keeps racing** while Purl brakes or stands still. | | `{ type: 'toggle-global-pause' }` | Pause/resume simulation for **both Purl and Loop**, including race timers. Preserve Purl's pre-pause brake state. This intent is emitted by an explicit pause control, never by a gesture. | Use elapsed seconds (`dt`) for movement, braking, smoothing, and jump physics; never multiply by an assumed frame rate. Integrate velocity across the braking interval, including its endpoint, so different refresh rates travel the same distance. Freeze simulation time during global pause and reset the animation-loop timestamp when resuming; a background-tab interval must not advance the race in one giant step. While globally paused, ignore steering/jump/brake requests and keep the pause button usable. Drive stride phase from **actual distance traveled**, not a free-running animation clock. Blend into an idle pose once Purl is stopped; do not keep feet running while the root is stationary. The opponent's movement and animation continue during the player-only brake. A late landing while braking must respect grounded physics and the requested stop state. ## Accessible controls and CSS Use real buttons so keyboard, assistive technology, mouse, and switch users have equivalents. Keep controls visible and sufficiently large, use clear focus styles, and update the brake/pause labels and `aria-pressed` values from actual engine state. If adding keyboard shortcuts, skip events from text inputs and editable content, and prevent repeated keydown toggles. ```html
``` Apply `touch-action: none` **before** contacts begin, only to the gameplay surface; leave page navigation and controls usable. Viewport-width measurement uses layout CSS pixels, not physical device pixels. Do not add competing click/double-click/touch listeners to the surface. Keep one adapter mounted per active playfield. ## Checks Run `node --test code/touch-input.test.mjs` from the kit folder. The tests cover threshold boundaries, directional exclusivity, tap eligibility, UI interruption, multi-touch, cancellation/capture loss, disposal, and coalesced drag excursions. They validate logic and a simulated adapter, not device compatibility. Before release, check on real touch devices: scroll/zoom containment, fast swipes, two-finger contact, interrupted gestures, UI buttons, background/resume, braking while jumping, and frame-rate-independent movement. # Touch input handoff `touch-input.mjs` is a small, dependency-free browser ES module. It emits immutable intentions; the game engine owns movement, animation, collision, and race state. Serve these files with the rest of the game; no CDN or runtime network request is needed. Browser ES modules generally need an HTTP origin, so opening the HTML directly as `file://` is not a supported launch method. ## Exports | Export | Contract | | --- | --- | | `attachTouchInput(surface, onIntent, options?)` | Pointer Events adapter. Returns `{ reset, dispose }`; call `dispose()` when replacing the scene. | | `createGestureMachine(options?)` | DOM-free state machine with `down`, `move`, `up`, `cancel(pointerId, options?)`, `reset`. Each returns an array of zero or one intents. | | `classifyGesture(sample, options?)` | Pure classifier: `tap`, `left`, `right`, `jump`, `reserved`, or `none`. | | `swipeThreshold(viewportWidth, options?)` | Horizontal/vertical threshold in CSS pixels. | | `INTENTS` | `left`, `right`, `jump`, `togglePlayerBrake`, `toggleGlobalPause`. Buttons and other accessible controls use the same objects. | | `DEFAULTS` | Frozen gesture defaults; pass overrides only after device testing. | Pointer samples use `{ pointerId, x, y, time, viewportWidth }`. `down` also accepts `ignored: true`. Use CSS coordinates and a single monotonic millisecond clock (`performance.now()`). The adapter supplies these; it deliberately does not depend on browser event timestamp origins. The pure classifier takes `{ dx, dy, duration, maxDistance, viewportWidth }`, where `maxDistance` is the furthest excursion from the starting point. For capture loss while a pointer remains down, call `cancel(id, { retainPointer: true })`; ordinary `pointercancel` uses `cancel(id)`. ## Exact behavior The swipe threshold is 8% of viewport width, clamped to 24–72 CSS pixels. A swipe must have a dominant axis (1.2× the other axis). Each stroke resolves once on release. Left/right emit one steering intention; up emits **jump only**. Down is reserved and emits nothing. Ambiguous diagonals and subthreshold movements emit nothing. Double tap requires two taps of at most 200 ms, each staying within 10 CSS pixels of its start, with releases no more than 320 ms apart and starts within 24 CSS pixels. A single tap has no action. Swipes, long presses, drag-return gestures, UI input, cancellation, and multi-touch invalidate pending taps. After a double tap, a third tap starts a new pair. Two simultaneous contacts are never a double tap. Multi-touch cancels until every tracked contact lifts; the module does not interpret pinch gestures. UI elements marked `data-ui`, native buttons/links/form inputs, editable text, and `role="button"` are excluded. Interaction outside the surface also clears pending taps. Pointer capture, `pointercancel`, capture loss, page visibility, and focus loss are handled. Call `reset()` when switching modes or opening/closing a pause screen. ## Wire the engine Start Purl automatically at a **normal, brisk** running pace. Calibrate world speed to scenery, camera scale, obstacle spacing, and available reaction distance; this module intentionally specifies no numeric world speed. | Intent | Required engine response | | --- | --- | | `{ type: 'steer', direction: -1 or 1 }` | During a junction selection window, queue the corresponding branch and commit at the junction. Between junctions, update the lane target or smooth steering target. Do not treat a swipe as teleportation. | | `{ type: 'jump' }` | Request a jump subject to grounded/jump rules. Never also issue forward movement or a speed boost. | | `{ type: 'toggle-player-brake' }` | Toggle Purl's requested running/stopped state. Decelerate to rest over **0.18–0.25 seconds**; a second double tap resumes normal running. **Loop keeps racing** while Purl brakes or stands still. | | `{ type: 'toggle-global-pause' }` | Pause/resume simulation for **both Purl and Loop**, including race timers. Preserve Purl's pre-pause brake state. This intent is emitted by an explicit pause control, never by a gesture. | Use elapsed seconds (`dt`) for movement, braking, smoothing, and jump physics; never multiply by an assumed frame rate. Integrate velocity across the braking interval, including its endpoint, so different refresh rates travel the same distance. Freeze simulation time during global pause and reset the animation-loop timestamp when resuming; a background-tab interval must not advance the race in one giant step. While globally paused, ignore steering/jump/brake requests and keep the pause button usable. Drive stride phase from **actual distance traveled**, not a free-running animation clock. Blend into an idle pose once Purl is stopped; do not keep feet running while the root is stationary. The opponent's movement and animation continue during the player-only brake. A late landing while braking must respect grounded physics and the requested stop state. ## Accessible controls and CSS Use real buttons so keyboard, assistive technology, mouse, and switch users have equivalents. Keep controls visible and sufficiently large, use clear focus styles, and update the brake/pause labels and `aria-pressed` values from actual engine state. If adding keyboard shortcuts, skip events from text inputs and editable content, and prevent repeated keydown toggles. ```html

Viewport-width measurement uses layout CSS pixels, not physical device pixels. Do not add competing click/double-click/touch listeners to the surface. Keep one adapter mounted per active playfield. ## Checks Run `node --test code/touch-input.test.mjs` from the kit folder. ims=[i.resize((round(i.width*H/i.height),H)) for i in ims]+[ov.resize((round(ov.width*H/ov.height),H))]
